text: Ninety years later, in Britain, a company made the same mistake with something far more expensive: airplane tickets.

Hoover's British business was struggling. In August 1992, it made an offer to customers in Britain and Ireland: spend 100 pounds on its products, get two free return flights to Europe. Then it added New York and Orlando.

The cheapest vacuum that qualified cost 119 pounds. The tickets were worth a lot more. People did the math. Stores sold out, and reportedly a market for barely-used vacuums appeared. By March 1993, about two hundred thousand people had claimed flights.
Hoover wanted to sell vacuums. It rewarded buying a vacuum. But the reward was bigger than the thing it was attached to — so people weren't buying vacuums anymore. They were buying flights.

Travel agents couldn't keep up. Customers waited, complained, and one angry customer went all the way to Iowa to confront the owner at its shareholders' meeting. Trading standards officers later found no fraud — just that Hoover had "grossly miscalculated" how many people would say yes. The owner, Maytag, paid for charter planes, removed three Hoover bosses, and took about 60 million dollars in charges in 1993. Two years later, it sold Hoover Europe. Court cases over the flights dragged on until 1998.
